items.title: Diablo IV: A Review in Four Acts

items.content_html:
Preface: By Three They Come

The Diablo IV cinematic reveal trailer, unveiled at BlizzCon 2019, intoned an old prophecy over images of blood and bone: "By three they come." Blizzard meant the three Prime Evils — Diablo, Mephisto, Baal — returning to consume Sanctuary. They didn't know they were also writing the blueprint for their own game's redemption arc.

Three years. Three directors. Three versions of the same game. Patch 3.0. A trilogy of expansions concluding with the Lord of Hatred himself. The symmetry is almost supernaturally neat, and it reframes what could otherwise be read as a story of corporate mismanagement into something almost mythologically inevitable. Sanctuary was always going to be saved by three. It just turned out the heroes were wearing Blizzard lanyards.

This review is told in four acts: launch, Season 4, Vessel of Hatred, and Lord of Hatred. Each one a different game. Each one a different Blizzard. And by the end — finally, improbably — something worth defending.

Act I — Launch (June 2023): The Gilded Corpse

The critics were besotted. Diablo IV achieved an OpenCritic score of 89 from 75 critic reviews, with 99% of reviewers recommending it. Metacritic landed at 88, with GameSpot giving it an 8 and IGN a 9, both praising its presentation, gameplay, and loot. Blizzard was credited with taking twenty years of design lessons and distilling them into a game with a gripping story, phenomenal graphics, and combat built on genuine intricacy and depth.

The professional press reviewed the campaign. Players reviewed the game.

And the players were furious. Before the ink on the review scores had even dried, the cracks opened. The campaign — extraordinary, dark, cinematic, a genuine return to the gothic soul of Diablo II — ended, and what players found on the other side was a hollowed-out live-service scaffolding dressed up as an endgame. A repetitive endgame loop, underwhelming loot systems, and limited social features like trading and leaderboards, combined with frustrations over progression stagnation, created a challenging environment almost immediately. Too many endgame builds felt like slightly more powerful versions of what you had already been running from level one. You could only cast Frost Nova or Whirlwind so many times before you started looking for alternatives — and the alternatives were significantly weaker, similarly repetitive, or both.

Then Season 1 arrived, and Blizzard did the unthinkable: they made it worse. Nearly every change in patch 1.1 made the game worse — DPS for all classes was slashed, survivability gutted — and none of them were actually balanced against each other. Sorcerers, already the weakest class, became practically unplayable in higher-level content. The backlash was so heavy that Blizzard addressed it directly in a Campfire Chat livestream, promising more transparency going forward. The Metacritic user scores collapsed — the PS5 version hit 1.8 from over 5,000 user ratings, the PC version 2.2 from over 7,000. A $70 game with a battle pass and a cosmetics shop where a single class-specific armor set cost $28 — more expensive, Reddit noted, than Overwatch 2 skins.

When Diablo IV finally arrived on Steam in October 2023, the accumulated resentment was waiting. Within 24 hours of the Steam launch, reviews sat at 58% positive — firmly "Mixed" — and the game peaked at under 2,500 concurrent players despite being one of the year's biggest releases. Steam players were blunter than any critic had dared to be. One review, widely upvoted, read: "During my childhood Blizzard couldn't get it wrong — as an adult, they can't get it right." Another noted: "The endgame does not compete at all with Path of Exile in terms of content or item complexity." On the Battle.net forums and Steam discussions, a recurring theme emerged: "This one is an unfinished mess, full of greedy microtransactions and time wasting practices to increase monthly player engagement."

The professional critics had reviewed the trailer Blizzard wanted to sell. The players had paid $70 to live in the game afterward.

This was Diablo IV at launch: a 4 out of 10 dressed in a 10 out of 10 coat.

Act II — Season 4: Loot Reborn (May 2024): The First Apology

Season 4 did not arrive as a content season. It arrived as an institutional act of contrition — the first honest acknowledgment that the game shipped broken.

Fan reception was overwhelmingly positive, with some players even claiming this season was "the real Diablo 4." Critically, Season 4 was the first to be extensively playtested by the community on a public test realm — something used in World of Warcraft and Diablo III but conspicuously absent for Diablo IV's previous seasons. That feedback made it into the game from day one, rather than arriving in emergency patches weeks later.

The loot system was overhauled. The grind was rebalanced. The game started breathing again. Players who had written Sanctuary off returned and found something that resembled what they had been promised in 2019. It was not yet a great game — the structural complaints, the thin endgame, the sense that the whole thing was jury-rigged season to season — all remained. But Season 4 proved something crucial: the team could listen. It was a down payment on a promise that had been broken several times already. Whether Blizzard would honor it remained, at that point, genuinely unclear.

Act III — Vessel of Hatred (October 2024): The Middle Child

Vessel of Hatred launched to a respectable 84/100 on Metacritic, with critics praising the gradual quality-of-life improvements that had made Diablo IV a smoother game by the time of the expansion's release. The new Spiritborn class was a genuine creative triumph — fluid, inventive, and generous with build diversity in a way the original classes had never been. The Mercenary system added warmth to solo play. The Undercity offered structured co-op challenge. One critic noted that "we have a much more different and packed Diablo IV than we had a year ago" and that the time had come to try it again.

But the players who had been there since launch were not so easily won. The expansion's campaign — the thing a $40 purchase most needed to justify itself — was widely felt as hollow. The pacing of events and outcomes felt unearned. It all felt like a setup, which is what some seasons should be for — not a paid expansion. The story was largely forgettable, more scaffolding for the next chapter than a satisfying narrative in its own right. Seasonal activities in the new Nahantu zones were mirrored in the original regions, and the new lands often felt empty as a result.

Players on Reddit and Steam were divided and vocal. Some called it a necessary course correction. Others felt that paying $40 to be told "wait until next year" was precisely the pattern they had learned not to trust. The fundamental problem — three different creative visions stapled together across years of chaotic development — had not been solved. It had merely been papered over with a new jungle zone and a very fun poison build.

Vessel of Hatred was the middle child of this trilogy in every sense: competent, somewhat overlooked, and carrying the weight of both what came before and the promise of what was supposed to come next.

Act IV — Lord of Hatred (April 2026): Version 3.0. The 1.0 We Were Promised.

The Diablo IV cinematic reveal trailer said by three they come. It took three years, three directors, and patch 3.0 for the game to finally arrive.

Lord of Hatred is one of the best expansions in the history of the Diablo saga — a magnificent conclusion to the Mephisto storyline, with a campaign of pure intensity, epic scale, genuine drama, and surprises you would not expect from a franchise that spent its first three years tripping over its own shoelaces. The two new classes are fantastic additions, complemented by a comprehensive redesign of every existing class's skill trees.

The loot filter — requested since before the game launched, ignored for years — is finally here, and it is robust. Rules, triggers, modifiers, the works. The overlay map, also long-requested, is now permanent. Unique items can be tempered. Their secondary stats roll variably, meaning finding the same Unique twice can now meaningfully matter. These two changes alone make the item chase feel purposeful in a way it never has before. The skill trees have been rebuilt across all classes — more than 40 reworked choices, 80 additional options, up to 83 available Skill Points. The Horadric Cube returns as a full crafting system. Critically, lower-rarity items are no longer automatically worthless in the endgame.

The critical response was strong. Reviewers called it a massive step forward in endgame content, new classes, and a campaign that reached emotional highs no one would have expected from this game. Game Informer called it an exceptional cherry on top of Diablo IV, cementing the entire package as among the best action RPGs of the generation. Icy Veins, reflecting the player community's own exhausted relief, concluded that Lord of Hatred is Diablo IV at its best — the story takes real risks, the Warlock is a fantastic addition, the Paladin fits right in, War Plans give the endgame genuine structure, and the quality-of-life improvements are things players had been requesting since before the game launched.

The player response echoed it. Lord of Hatred brought Diablo IV its highest concurrent player count on Steam in 2026, and early Steam reviews ran 123 positive to 31 negative. Not the explosive return of Vessel of Hatred's launch numbers, but something arguably more meaningful: steady, earned confidence from a community that had learned not to trust this game easily.

And yet — and this is the honest part — Lord of Hatred is a truly successful expansion, but one that highlights once again how Diablo IV's flaws stem directly from its base version. Blizzard has listened, and what it is implementing is a genuine process of rebuilding its iconic hack-and-slash. But it is still a rebuild. A new player arriving today will feel three different games layered on top of each other: the somber, grounded campaign of 2023; Vessel of Hatred's tentative second act; and Lord of Hatred's confident stride. The seams are real. The journey is visible. The destination, finally, is worth the trip.

The Case for an In-Game Codex

Diablo IV's greatest unacknowledged problem is legibility. Across three years of seasonal updates, expansion systems, reworked skill trees, Paragon boards, Glyphs, Aspects, Tempers, Talismans, Charms, the Horadric Cube, loot filters, and set bonuses — the game has accumulated a vocabulary that it expects players to learn entirely from external wikis, Discord servers, and content creators. This is a design debt that compounds with every expansion.

What the game needs is a living, in-game Codex — something in the spirit of Civilization's Civilopedia. Not tooltips. Not loading screen tips. A proper reference, accessible at any moment, that explains every mechanic, every stat interaction, every system clearly and completely. One that treats its players as intelligent adults who simply haven't memorized three years of patch notes.

The lore dimension of this matters just as much. Diablo's world-building is extraordinary — centuries of scripture, prophecy, corrupted theology, and cosmic horror that most players will never fully encounter because it is scattered across item descriptions, ambient dialogue, and optional journal entries that disappear the moment you walk away. A catalogue of cinematics, dialogue, and lore entries that players could revisit freely — for theory-crafting, for story analysis, for the kind of deep fan investment that keeps communities alive for decades — would be transformative. Sanctuary deserves to be studied. Give players the tools to do it.

On the Music: An Overdue Love Letter

The Diablo IV soundtrack has, since launch, been quietly one of the finest scores in the action RPG genre — a sprawling, layered composition that earns its place in the franchise's legendary sonic lineage. The good news, for those who want to carry Sanctuary with them: the complete catalogue spanning every Diablo game, titled "The Music of Diablo," is available on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, Deezer, and more — from the eerie tones of the original game through to the cinematic orchestration of Diablo IV. And now, the Lord of Hatred Original Soundtrack — 32 songs across more than 2.5 hours, composed by Ted Reedy and Ryan Amon — is also available on all major streaming platforms.

This music holds up magnificently outside the game. It is moody, orchestral, occasionally brutal, and never anything less than atmospheric. That it has not yet received a physical CD release for collectors remains a genuine oversight — and one that Blizzard should correct. A franchise of this legacy and this sonic ambition deserves shelf space.

Final Verdict

Diablo IV launched in 2023 as a 4 out of 10 in every dimension that determines whether a live service game survives — endgame, systems design, respect for player time, and trust — wearing the disguise of a campaign that deserved a 9. The professional critics reviewed the disguise. The players paid to live inside the game afterward, and they let Blizzard know what they found there, loudly, repeatedly, and with a vocabulary that made Metacritic user scores look like crime scenes.

Three years later — three directors, three acts, patch 3.0, and an ancient prophecy accidentally fulfilled — Diablo IV has earned a genuine 8 out of 10. Not because every problem is solved. The three-era seams are still visible to anyone paying attention. The in-game knowledge infrastructure is still inadequate. The cosmetics shop is still priced for people who have lost the ability to feel regret. But the game that exists now — with Lord of Hatred's campaign, its overhauled systems, its two excellent new classes, its finally-present loot filter, its returning Horadric Cube — is a confident, content-rich, mechanically rewarding experience that a new player can step into today and genuinely love.

The reveal trailer said it. It just took the full three to deliver on it.

By three they come.
